title: Why Long-Context Speed Comes Down to Prefill and KV Heads
hook: Everyone benchmarks token-generation speed. A community test of 13 models at 65K-128K context found that's the wrong number — prefill dominates, and KV head count beats parameter count.
key_points: Benchmarked 13 local models at 65K-128K context specifically for agentic workloads (tool use, coding agents, RAG), not chat.
Prefill (processing the long input context before generating anything) dominates total latency far more than token-generation speed (tg128), the metric most people fixate on.
KV head count predicts long-context speed better than raw parameter count — architecture choices around attention matter more than model size at long context.
Ran on consumer/prosumer hardware (RX 7900 XT, llama.cpp/llama-bench), making the findings directly actionable for people running local models.
content_html: Most local-LLM benchmarks lead with token-generation speed — tokens per second once the model is already talking. For agentic workloads like tool use, coding agents, and RAG, where the context window fills up before the model says a word, that number turns out to be measuring the wrong thing.
extra_html: This community benchmark tested 13 models at 65K-128K context specifically for agentic use cases, running on consumer/prosumer hardware (an RX 7900 XT via llama.cpp/llama-bench). The headline finding: prefill time — processing the long input context before any generation starts — dominates total latency far more than generation speed does, once the context window is actually full, which flips the usual "tg128 as headline metric" framing on its head. The second finding is architectural: KV head count predicted long-context speed better than raw parameter count did, meaning attention-design choices matter more than sheer model size once you're operating at long context. For anyone choosing a model to run locally for agentic work, the practical upshot is to check prefill throughput and KV-head design, not just the parameter count on the model card. Posted to r/LocalLLaMA, 2026-07-05.

related.title: The KV Cache & Continuous Batching
related.hook: Generating one token reuses every prior key and value - that growing cache is why LLM inference is memory-bound, and continuous batching is how servers fight back.

related.title: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)
related.hook: Split the difference between multi-head and multi-query attention: share KV heads across groups of query heads and get most of the memory savings with little quality loss.

related.title: Multi-Query Attention: Faster Decoding
related.hook: Share one key/value head across all query heads - the KV cache shrinks by a factor of H and decoding gets dramatically faster with barely any quality cost.
